subsubtopic: SITUATION IN MONTREAL EAST-PROPOSED ACTION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after two months of uninterrupted and repeated requests from Members of the Opposition and the Montreal East survival committee, the Government has just announced the creation of a six-Minister Cabinet committee to provide assistance to the Montreal region, mainly to Montreal East which is now experiencing a situation likely to result in the loss of 5,000 jobs.
For openers, Mr. Speaker, as a Member of the House and one of the people responsible for the survival committee, I would like to serve immediate notice on those Ministers that the workers will simply not stand still while this third committee runs around in circles. I would also advise the committee and its chairman, the President of the Treasury Board, that one more study is not going to help Montreal East. First, the Government must give Montreal East a Zone-IV designation to make all industries and workers eligible for the best grant programs. Second, the Government must cancel the Gulf sale to Ultramar and let Gaz metropolitain buy the refinery and protect jobs. Third, the Government must immediately award contracts to Montreal East's Canadian Vickers under the TRUMP or Multi-Ship programs. Fourth, the Government must immediately convene CN, VIA Rail and CP representatives so that they may award contracts to Bombardier, Canadian Steel Wheel and La Forge. Mr. Speaker, on Monday-

subsubtopic: CANADIAN IMPERIAL BANK OF COMMERCE-TREATMENT OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning's Globe and Mail reports that the Canadian Imperial Bank of
Commerce intends "to split its shares and increase its dividends as signs of a turnabout become more apparent". This bank can afford to raise the dividends on shares but refuses to deal with its employees in a fair and equitable manner. The Commerce is well known for maintaining a ghetto of low-paid employees, the majority of whom are women, and of practising tactics of intimidation toward pro-union workers and favouritism toward others.
On a number of occasions the CIBC has been found guilty of unfair labour practices. I have written the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) asking him to improve labour relations within banks through stronger legislation. This week the Minister responded to me by indicating his unwillingness to take such a step. I again urge the Government to set up an inquiry into the labour practices of all banks and to improve the Canada Labour Code by introducing meaningful first-contract legislation so that the banks will be forced to negotiate fairly with their employees.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is becoming a land of opportunity again. Since this Government was elected, 416,000 jobs have been added to the labour force, 83,000 of which were added in November alone. The unemployment rate has fallen from 11.6 per cent in September, 1984, to 10.2 per cent now. Youth unemployment has declined more than two full percentage points. The total of unemployed people has fallen by 148,000 persons. The job-creation rate since the last general election has been four times better than the job-creation rate in the entire 55 months of the previous regime.
Not only is this a trend across the country but, according to the Canada Employment Centre, in Canada's seventh largest city, of Scarborough, this national trend is evident locally. Since September, 1984, the number of Scarborough employers seeking help has increased by one-third over that of the previous 14 months.
This should not be written off as a world-wide trend with no Canadian component. According to current statistics, Canada is reducing unemployment faster than any other western industrial country except The Netherlands. This dramatically improved employment picture shows that we are fulfilling the commitment we made to the Canadian people-that we would renew the economy and that we would do it by making this a

December 6, 1985
country for doing business, for making investments, and for expanding opportunity.
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, as 1985 draws to a close I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the youth of Canada for the outstanding contribution they have made during this International Youth Year. In addition, I would like to commend the Government of Canada and the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) for the positive programs put forward to assist the youth of Canada with their varied and imaginative projects.
Prior to my election to the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, I was actively involved as an educator for 31 years. During that time I had the privilege of working with thousands of young people in both academic and social surroundings. They are genuinely committed to Canada's future. More youth in Canada today are in school and are staying longer. Clearly today's Canadian youth represent the best educated and best trained generation our country has ever produced.
One day, many of the leaders of today's youth will be the leaders of our various levels of Government and industries, making the difficult yet necessary decisions which will affect the economic prosperity and social activity of our great country. It is our duty as parliamentarians to ensure that not only our young people but youth throughout the world inherit a future which is filled with hope and a global security secured in peace and compassion.
It is in this spirit that I urge the Government to make representations at the United Nations to have 1986-1996 declared "International Decade for Youth". It would be a fitting tribute to our youth-
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the Hustler magazine issue is a classic example of the hypocrisy of the Government. It claims it is concerned about the importation of pornography into Canada. It says it cares about the issue and calls it an issue of paramount urgency. Yet the Government has done absolutely nothing with respect to this
disgusting and revolting magazine, in particular the December issue of the magazine.
Last Friday the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) promised the House that a report would be forthcoming by Monday. Some five days later we still do not have that report. It would lead one to conclude that the Government simply does not care about this most important issue.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) suggests we should simply ignore the matter and it might go away. However, that is not the proper course of action as far as we are concerned. Definite action must be taken immediately. The magazine entered Canada because of the gross negligence of the Government. We now find that the Government is planning to cut back 1,152 jobs in the Department of Customs and Excise. While we need more Customs inspectors the Government is planning on cutting back.
The Conservative Government should hang its head in shame for not taking immediate steps to ensure that this magazine is taken off the shelves. Mr. Speaker-
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: BIG NUMBER OF JOBS CREATED SINCE ELECTION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the latest employment figures show that the Government is making every effort to meet its commitment to create jobs. Last November, 83,000 new jobs, most of them full time, were created thanks to Government policies.
Since September 1984, when Canadians voted for a new direction from a Conservative Government, we have helped 416,000 Canadians to find jobs, 416,000 Canadians who were previously unemployed and who would certainly not have found work if a Liberal Government had been in power.
Mr. Speaker, even the Opposition with its complaints and criticisms will admit that this is an unprecedented figure. The Government is living up to its slogan of jobs, jobs, jobs. Unemployment insurance benefits have gone down by 5 per cent since last August.
And it is not only in relation with job creation that this Government is putting Canada back on the map. I would like to point out that the federal deficit for the third quarter amounted to a seasonally adjusted figure of $25 billion, which is 19.4 per cent lower than during the previous quarter.
This Government is restoring the Canadian public's confidence in the economy, Mr. Speaker. We are doing our job!
December 6, 1985

Mr. Speaker, today I wish all my colleagues a very happy St. Nicholas Day. The tradition of that fine old soul who cared so much for all children reflects the best of human nature. It is no wonder that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his wife chose to name their newest son Nicholas.
Nicholas is a very fortunate little baby who gets to go to work with his mother. Mila is a very unusual working mother who, unlike most women, has the opportunity to bring her son into the workplace. We presume Nick's father is sharing the parenting during his frequent absences from the House. Mila feels she and Nicholas are advocates for child care which will magically take place on its own. Will every plant have an assembly line of cribs alongside the word processors?
The need for accessible, affordable day care is urgent. Women are working hard and carrying double burdens. Some 60 per cent of working women are married and one-half of their families would be poor if they were not in the workforce. Two income are necessary today just to survive.
Children must not be victims of poverty. We must provide quality child care now. If Mila Mulroney wishes to play an advocate role she should insist the federal Government move quickly to ensure universal, publicly-funded day care for all of Canada's children.
* *
*

Mr. Speaker, following upon commitments made during the last election campaign, this Progressive Conservative Government has taken concrete steps to rationalize and enhance the role of Crown corporations in the Canadian community of 1985.
This party has always favoured the existence and operations of those corporations provided they agreed with our national interests. In the course of that review, we have reached the conclusion that some of those corporations were no longer serving the purposes intended or that their objectives had been reached and their participation in national life was therefore no longer required or desirable.
This is why we proceeded with the winding up of four inoperative Crown corporations; with the winding up of corporations that no longer answered the purposes of public policy; and also with the sale of Northern Transportations Company Limited, Canadian Arsenals and de Havilland as well as Canadian Government interests in the Canada Development Corporation.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, in addition to bringing nearly half a billion dollars into the Federal treasury, those sales, sale proposals and winding ups will reduce by some $700 million this year the Canadian Government's financial needs. They will also help us reduce the deficit by another $350 million during the 1985-86 fiscal year.
Moreover, those moves show that we have no intention of maintaining an unnecessary presence in industries that do not require direct public sector involvement.
I regret to inform the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: SALE OF BUFFALO MEAT FROM HERD EXPOSED TO TUBERCULOSIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture, it concerns the health of Canadians and the damage inflicted upon the agricultural industry by the neglect of the Minister of Agriculture. Can the Minister confirm that two Conservative Members of Parliament from Ontario, namely, the Hon. Member for Peterborough and the Hon. Member for Simcoe North, met with the Minister and made representations to him concerning the infected buffalo meat? Can he further confirm that those Members of Parliament were concerned as early as October 15 that TB infected meat was going to be permitted for sale, potentially jeopardizing the indusjtry and damaging the health of Canadians?

subsubtopic: SALE OF BUFFALO MEAT FROM HERD EXPOSED TO TUBERCULOSIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome the opportunity to respond. I apologize for not being in the House yesterday. However, I was in the marathon meetings with representatives of the Ontario Flue Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board, as well as the companies, attempting to arrive at a settlement for the 1985 crop. Indeed, I am pleased to report progress.
1 do appreciate the response of my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in taking notice of the questions, and I want to acknowledge as well the representations made to me on the dates to which the Hon. Member refers by my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North and the Hon. Member for Peterborough. In addition to that, if my memory serves me correctly, I believe representation was also made to me by the Hon. Member for Timiskaming.
Within seconds of notification of this information, I contacted my senior officials. I requested them to apply the letter of the Act with respect to this particular situation. 1 can assure the Hon. Member that we have one of the finest meat and food

December 6, 1985
Oral Questions
inspection services in this country. It is widely recognized throughout the entire industry and it is respected throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Minister knew of the potential health hazard, and in view of the fact that the health test being done was not even completed as late as yesterday, my question is very simple. Why did the Minister allow the meat to be sold when he did not have full knowledge of what the health implications were? Could he also tell us if this is another case of the Government giving the benefit of the doubt to the corporate sector against the health of Canadians? Is this another case of the tuna affair repeated?

Mr. Speaker, that is utter nonsense, as well as most of the observations made by the Hon. Member. He should know-but I can tell by some of his comments he doesn't know-that the Meat Inspection Act, which has been in effect for 75 years, and which was amended on May 8 of this year with the support of all Parties, does not extend ministerial authority to me to overrule my inspectors.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Concerning again the tainted buffalo meat, the Minister was aware that this meat was not to be sold abroad. Exporting that meat would have been prohibited. Importing it would also have been prohibited. If it is not good enough for foreigners, why is it good enough for Canadians? Is the Minister using the same logic that his former colleague the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans used in making his decision?

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member was aware of the provisions in the Act and of the spirit of the international convention, he would not pose that question because for a good number of years that practice and procedure have been used. If a carcass goes through the inspection and requires additional inspection; i.e., a lesion is found in the carcass, then, of course, it is condemned. If a lesion is found within an organ the proper procedure is always followed, as it was in this case, and it is sent to a laboratory for testing.
The Hon. Member indicates that the tests have been completed. They have not. They were sent to a laboratory in Nepean where a series of tests is carried out. I am advised that the results of the final tests will not be known for four, five, or six weeks.
That's ridiculous.

All of the tests that have been completed have come back negative. It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that during the debate on that issue the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is reported at page 4536 of Hansard as saying that:
Liberal Members do in fact acknowledge that the meat inspection system in this country is indeed excellent.
Where does he stand? Is he for it or against it?
It was, before you came along.

subtopic: PROVISIONS OF MEAT INSPECTION ACT AND REGULATIONS
PROVISIONS OF MEAT INSPECTION ACT AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government obviously does not learn from its mistakes. It is not satisfied with unloading tainted tuna on to the Canadian public. It is now questionable buffalo meat-surf and turf.
Is the Minister aware of Section 474 of the Meat Inspection Act and regulations which state that, if any lesions are found, total condemnation of the herd is required?

subtopic: PROVISIONS OF MEAT INSPECTION ACT AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very much aware of the Act and of the regulation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PROVISIONS OF MEAT INSPECTION ACT AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why not act?

subtopic: PROVISIONS OF MEAT INSPECTION ACT AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I say again that I have full and complete confidence in the meat inspection system in this country. Ministerial authority is not given to over-rule my inspectors. I simply ask them to apply the full letter of the law and, if they find anything questionable, to err on the side of health and public safety. This course of action has been followed for 75 years. It has served the industry, the Canadian public, and the international marketplace well. There is a great deal of respect for this system across the country and in the international marketplace, although it may not be shared by Members opposite.

Mr. Speaker, lesions indicating the possible presence of tuberculosis were found in six of these animals. Yet the meat was released before the final tests were completed. If the Minister is satisfied to say that there was no tuberculosis present in these animals, why are the tests still on-going?

It is very simple, Mr. Speaker. The tests have nothing to do with the condemnation of the meat, but have everything to do with wiping out tuberculosis in the bovine herd across the country. That is the reason for the test of the organs. I think we should recognize and compliment the meat inspectors across the country because they contributed in a major way to the very rapid and significant decrease of bovine TB in humans.
December 6, 1985

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Agriculture. When lesions are found in a carcass or on the vital organs of a carcass, is it not standard practice for the inspectors to set that carcass aside until the laboratory work on those lesions has been completed? Why was that not done in this case?
To be perfectly honest with you, Mr. Speaker, I cannot give the Hon. Member a definite answer to this.
That's ridiculous.

As 1 have indicated, I was informed of this situation at the beginning. 1 have sought advice subsequent to that as late as yesterday and this morning. I am informed that the normal, traditional procedures were used in this case as they are used day in and day out. Thousands of livestock carcasses move through our slaughter plants on a daily or weekly basis.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. In another New Brunswick case the Prime Minister said that it seemed "pretty damn obvious" to him that a certain parcel of product should not have been released before the laboratory tests were completed. This is also the case in this instance. Does the Prime Minister honestly believe that he can retain a Cabinet Minister who will allow Canadians to eat meat that may have been diseased, who released it for the use of Canadian consumers before the laboratory tests on a herd that was found to be tubercular were completed so that we knew whether or not these particular carcasses were affected?
[DOT] (U25)
Mr. Speaker, 1 always welcome the opportunity to answer questions, but 1 welcome this one with a little more enthusiasm.
I wasn't asked of you.
Let me indicate that our record is the finest in the world.
Not to me it isn't.

1 said that we have had 75 years of this, and the normal accepted procedures in this case have been followed as they were in the last 75 years.
Hon. Members should be aware that there has not been one single documented case since the introduction of the Meat Inspection Act, the application of that Act and the application of those regulations by our federal meat inspection officers in the last 75 years-

You could be the first.
Oral Questions

-of bovine tuberculosis transmitted to humans from meat that has been inspected by our inspectors.
I think that is a tremendous record ando ne that should be acknowledged.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, would the Minister explain specifically why those five or six carcasses in which lesions were found in their vital organs were not set aside?

Mr. Speaker, I told the Hon. Member that 1 could not give him a direct, honest answer, and I want to give him an honest answer. For all 1 know, at the moment, maybe what the Hon. Member is asking about was done. Give me an opportunity to find out. Give me 15 minutes after Question Period and 1 will give you the answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what an incredible admission of incompetence, for the Minister to stand in the House and say: "I don't know why but I am perfectly sure everything is fine with that meat".
Ask a question.

The Minister's Pontius Pilate routine won't wash. The buck stops with him.
Why, in the face of representations from Members of Parliament, representations from the buffalo herders industry-
It is Question Period, not debate.

Why did the Minister allow that meat to go to market without having the results of those tests on six animals, tests, incidentally, which indicate from the animal that died in New Brunswick that TB was present in that herd? Why was that meat product allowed to go on the plates of Canadian consumers?

Mr. Speaker, if I had a choice between following the recommendations and the advice of my inspectors or that of the Hon. Member, it would be a very easy decision. I would choose and would rather err on the side of competence, and I would err on the side of a proven record.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have just heard from the Minister is that when two Members of Parliament representing buffalo herders in their districts tell a cabinet Minister in the Government that

December 6, 1985
Oral Questions
their people say there is a problem, you don't listen. What you are saying-
Order. I believe the Hon. Member had a long question the first time. Could he now ask his question, please?

Is the Minister of Agriculture telling the House that he is satisfied that the inspection process that allowed this buffalo meat to go to market, in the absence of complete tests, is the same process and involves the same standards that are applied to all red meat inspection in this country? Is that what he is telling the House?

Mr. Speaker, briefly, that is exactly what I am telling the House, and I say it with a great deal of satisfaction and confidence. If there is any question in the Hon. Member's mind, there isn't in mine. Just look at the record. There is no question that the record is fantastic.
The Canadian people have been well served by it, I think the Government has been well served by it, and I am sure that I, as Minister of Agriculture, will be well served by it too.

[DOT] (M30)

Mr. Speaker, first it was Tunagate, and yesterday it was TB dinners. Now we have to add to the regulatory mess this Government has produced the importation of the pesticide alachlor after a previous Government ban.
Just who is running the ship at Agriculture Canada when, in spite of a ban, unspecified amounts of a cancer-causing pesticide already contaminating our drinking water are allowed into the country?
Mr. Speaker, I am in control of Agriculture Canada. I make no apologies for that whatsoever.

Mr. Speaker, let us see how accurate is the information which the Minister has available to him.
Will the Minister determine the whereabouts and the amount of alachlor presently in the country? Will he immediately place a complete embargo on its use and on the entry of any further supplies of it until the outcome of the Review Committee's activities is known?

Again, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is outdated. We have already done that. We took action, I believe, on February 25 this year.

[ Translation]

subtopic: INQUIRY WHY BUFFALO MEAT NOT USED FOR DOG FOOD

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY WHY BUFFALO MEAT NOT USED FOR DOG FOOD
speechtext:

Could the Minister tell the House how he had the nerve to allow this meat to reach the tables of Canada, after Government experts had said it should have been destroyed or used to make pet foods?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am aware of some observations that have been made across the country from various sources. 1 watched a comment or two made by a veterinarian, I believe, in western Canada and I immediately drew that information to the attention of my senior officials. I was told that these observations are made from time to time by various people in the industry and various people in the profession.
I am advised that the individual whom I saw has admitted that he is not an expert in the area of meat inspection.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF POSITIONS OF TWO MINISTERS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF POSITIONS OF TWO MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it strange that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans had disregarded his own officials' recommendations for returning the tuna to the shelves, while the Minister of Agriculture dares not overrule his officials' recommendations in order to protect public health.
How is it that we have this difference between the two Departments?
December 6, 1985

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF POSITIONS OF TWO MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to explain the difference. The only fact is we have an excellent record. We have the finest system in the world. 1 do not have ministerial discretion under the Act. I think that should provide the answer.
It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, that there is so much criticism contrary to what was said when we amended the Act on May 8. I have quoted the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I quote now the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre:
Members of Parliament, farmers, meat packers, processors and consumers are convinced that we have the makings of a very good meat inspection system.

If it is not the best in the world, it is certainly among the best in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. I find it very interesting and deeply disturbing. We now know the Minister knew about the situation in general on October 14. He has just stood in the House, and I want to verify this, to say that he did not know up until today, and still does not know, and is now telling the House of Commons and the people of Canada, that in spite of carcasses being found to be infected, what happened to those carcasses afterwards. Partly right, Mr. Speaker, but partly wrong.
Oh, oh!
It is pretty serious stuff.

What I have not clarified is whether the six carcasses having organs containing lesions were detained for a period of time. That is what I am saying. I have offered to supply the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre with that information.
Hon. Members mistakenly take for granted that simply because an animal entering a plant has a positive test it is infected with TB, but that is not the case. It may or may not be the case. As to the other inaccurate conclusions which Hon. Members are drawing that a trained qualified veterinarian can tell visually whether a lesion is active or is a TB lesion, that is not known until those organs are forwarded to a lab for tests. This is being done now.
Oral Questions
There are a series of tests, four or five to be exact, some of which take a long period of time. I understand there is one test for which the results are not yet in. Three or four tests on lesions from those animals have up to this point in time been negative.
With great respect, this is becoming too long. The Hon. Member for Oshawa has a supplementary question?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister on this important matter.
We now know the carcasses found to be contaminated were in fact sent to western Canada, sold in western Canada, and have now been eaten. We have an acknowledgement from the Minister that in the middle of October he was aware of the general circumstance. He has admitted now in the House that nothing was done to ensure the carcasses were destroyed, that he did not even pursue the matter to find out whether the meat was on the shelves, or what happened to it.
Does the Prime Minister accept this as responsible behaviour from a Minister? If he does not, will the Prime Minister take steps to change this Minister as he did with a previous Minister in the Tunagate affair?
It is pretty damned obvious that the meat should not have gone on the table.

Mr. Speaker, Parliament passed an Act of Parliament in 1907 which set out terms and conditions of the Act and set out its regulations. The law has worked perfectly over the ensuing 75 years. Earlier this year we took the initiative and amended the Act to legalize some of the practices and procedures which had been used over time by our meat inspectors, to give them legal authority to ensure greater public health and safety. I have difficulty with this, Mr. Speaker, but the Member must have respect for this Parliament and he must have respect for legislation passed by this Parliament, particularly if that legislation has worked so well over the years.
The Hon. Member must also accept the fact that that Act does not give me ministerial authority. I checked within seconds, less than a minute, but the only authority I have, which I utilized within seconds of being advised by three colleagues, was to call my senior officials. I was going to make them aware of the situation but they already knew about it. They already had these animals in detention and had known about the problem for a long time.
Hear, hear!
The Hon. Member for Scarborough East.

Sorry.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is certainly with a great deal of satisfaction that I address the House on the third reading stage of Bill C-74. Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections has had an opportunity to make an in-depth study of all questions related to this Bill.
In June 1985 1 had the honour to table, on behalf of the Government, the White Paper on Redistribution which the committee had considered before the parliamentary recess.
After weighing the committee recommendations, the Government made a number of amendments to the Bill. The Government took advantage of the committee proceedings on this Bill to re-examine certain basic questions and fine-tune some of its provisions.

I think the process undertaken with respect to this Bill is a worth-while example to keep in mind as the House proceeds with parliamentary reform. Parliamentarians were involved at the beginning of the development of the policy, as well as during consideration of its implications in public hearings of the committee. 1 am well satisfied that the committee was able to give ample and serious consideration to the implications of the Bill, both before it was introduced in the House and after it was referred to it by the House.
1 would like to take this opportunity to thank the members of the committee for their long and diligent efforts in ensuring that all parts of this country will, for the foreseeable future, have fair and equitable representation. I would particularly like to thank the Hon. Members for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), Algoma (Mr. Foster) and Churchill (Mr. Murphy), whose contributions were invaluable to the study of the Bill.
When the House was considering the report stage of the Bill it was my pleasure to be able to move two motions which I believe improve the Bill. One provides for faster growth of the size of the House of Commons after the first redistribution, but it has a negligible net result after the third redistribution for which we have population projections. In other words, we are fast tracking the increases.

As a result of this amendment to the basic formula, the seat distribution in the House will reflect more closely the national population ratio in each province.
Considering the many compromises which have been reached with respect to the principle of representation by

December 6, 1985

population, this measure is the only one under which the representation of each province is fair and equitable.
I want to assure all of my colleagues that the Government would not have agreed to such an amendment if it had in any way made the proportional representations of the provinces any worse, based on the current population projections. I can say with some confidence that the position of the provinces is improved after the redistribution, which will follow immediately upon the passage of this Act. And in subsequent redistributions, the proportion of representation of provinces is, in almost every case, enhanced over and above their current representation in the House.
Of course, the only estimate of the number of seats each province will be assigned, which is based on actual population figures, is that which is based on the 1981 census, and these estimates will only become a reality after the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commissions have done their work.

I was pleased to be able to move this amendment on behalf of the committee. Mr. Speaker, before I start I would like to announce that upon concluding my comments, I intend to move an amendment, and I am saying this so the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) will not be taken by surprise.
Typically, the debate on this subject, which is always an important one, also tends to be somewhat embarrassing when we are talking about redistribution, since often, provinces that should normally get more members get less, other provinces in the same position do not get the number to which they are entitled, and there are also provinces that should get fewer Members but get more because of certain provisions in the Constitution. We all know that under the Canadian Constitution, no province can have fewer Members than Senators. Thus, and I think this is a sign of healthy federalism, the Province of Prince Edward Island cannot have fewer than four Members because the Constitution clearly says it must have four Senators.
It is also true that these provisions in the Constitution Act may eventually protect the position of New Brunswick which has ten Senators and which from now on should never have fewer than ten Members. The same applies to Nova Scotia which now has eleven Members and ten Senators, and thus can never have fewer than ten Members, and Newfoundland, which has seven Members and can never have fewer than six because there are six Senators from Newfoundland.
Furthermore, there are large areas, like the Yukon, that would normally have only one Member or no Members at all, and which are given one because that is the absolute minimum. And we all know the Hon. Member for Yukon. As I said recently, the Northwest Territories are represented by one of the Members I see here in the House, sitting on the Government side. Normally, because of their numbers, the Northwest Territories should have only one Member, but for all kinds of reasons which I heartily approve, we have at least two Members from the Northwest Territories, even if they do not have the population to warrant that number.
So there is constitutional protection for some provinces, a certain understanding for the particular situation in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, and we must therefore conclude that what we have here is not the sacred principle of representation by population, since we already have quite a number of exceptions which l just mentioned. 1 repeat, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, for different reasons, and under the Constitution, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick in fact all the Maritime Provinces have safeguards, irrespective of their population.
If we had adopted the Bill tabled by the previous Government, we would have 310 Members after the next election. There was a lot of debate on this matter, because of the very quick progression from 310 to 343 or more in 1991 and 369 in the year 2001. And although the debate was quite heated
December 6, 1985

among Members of the various parties, it was not a partisan debate. There are a number of questions: Are we not progressing too quickly? Do we want a huge House where the Mari-times and francophone groups will be swallowed up completely? I will get back to the issue of Quebec francophones later on.
So we would have a House that would be far too big. But the previous Government had followed the legislation and was forced to have a number of Members under an older legislation which had been adopted when we had reached 282 seats in the House and which stipulated an increase to 310 and so on.
I was here at the time when there were 264 seats and there was a new distribution. 1 had tried to make a point at the time and failed . . . and we saw the House go from 264 seats to 282 and Quebec obtained one out of the 18 new seats. I felt at the time that the number of seats in the House should have been frozen forever at 264 and that through comprehensive constitutional amendments, we should have continued to protect the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, the Maritimes, while adding a new factor, that is recognizing the fact that Quebec is, for historical reasons, the national homeland of Quebecers and Francophones; however, I failed to convince the House at that time. Now, we should have been presented with a Bill which, if we did nothing, would increase the number of seats to 310 by the next election. The map is already drawn. All parties, the Liberals, the Progressive Conservatives and the socialists have discussed this issue and agreed that it was out of the question for the number of seats to increase immediately from 310 to 343, 369, etc.
So, at one point, and 1 would not want to put the blame on anybody, it was agreed that the sacred principle of proportional representation could be discarded for economic reasons and in order to protect the Maritimes, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and that we should adopt a new formula.
The Hon. President of Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) put forward a first proposal. He said: We will not increase the number of seats to 310, 342, 343, or 363. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak on the third reading debate on Bill C-74, an Act which will affect redistribution for the next number of elections. Before I speak about the Act itself, I would like to spend a fair bit of time on the amendment before us. In introducing the amendment, the Liberal Member who spoke on behalf of his caucus said that the Government had changed the rules at the last moment and that for some reason the Liberal Party was unaware of the amendments and felt now at third reading that it was necessary to introduce a motion to send this matter back to the committee.
Let me explain some of the history of this particular piece of legislation. This legislation was introduced by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for pre-study last May and the committee had a chance to study it in June. It was brought back to the House this fall, at which time we had one-day's debate and sent the matter to committee for further study. It was the request of the NDP and Liberal caucuses
December 6, 1985

that a number of witnesses should appear before us to talk particularly about fairness within this legislation.
Quite a few speakers from all parts of Canada and from most provinces including the Province of Quebec, came before us to discuss the proposal. The one thing that the vast majority of witnesses who came before us said was that the legislation was unfair to the provinces that have growing populations. Not only had a cap been put on the size to which the House can grow but those provinces with growing populations like Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia would, once the national quota had been decided, only be given one-half of the increase to which they would have been entitled. In other words, if the Province of Ontario were to receive 10 more seats because of its growth in population, it would only be given five more seats. If the Province of Alberta were to be entitled to two seats, it would receive only one. If the Province of British Columbia found itself in a situation in which it should receive four seats, it would receive only two. Almost every witness who came before the committee made that very point, and for very good reason. We were guaranteeing Prince Edward Island four seats. We were guaranteeing Quebec a certain number of seats and that that number would never decrease. We were guaranteeing Manitoba and Saskatchewan that they would keep the number of seats which they presently have regardless of what happens to the population of their provinces. Proportionately, if the Province of Quebec decreased in size in terms of Canada's population, when compared with the rest of the country, it would maintain its 75 seats, which is what it has at the present time. However, the large provinces, the ones which are growing, would be doubly penalized. First of all, they have no guarantees that they should increase at the rate by which they should increase according to strict representation by population, this was being denied because we were guaranteeing Quebec and almost all the other provinces that they would never lose seats. That was one penalty which was imposed by the legislation in its original form.
The second penalty is one I mentioned earlier. That is to say if British Columbia, as a result of this Government's devised formula, was entitled to four more seats, as a result of a clause in the original legislation, it would only be given two more. In other words, not only would those provinces not receive the six or eight seats which they should receive if we were going strictly by representation by population, but after the new formula came in, which guaranteed the non-growing provinces a certain number of seats they would lose, they would receive half of the seats to which they would be entitled.
We brought witnesses before the committee who made the same point. They said that something had to be done in order to protect the small provinces. They said that we had to accept the senatorial floor and that it seemed reasonable to accept the new grandfathering clause. This clause brought in other provinces in order that their present representation in the House of Commons would be protected, and the minimum number of seats which they had would always remain at that number.

We must remember that under existing legislation the report of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commission, once it goes through the process of studying the boundaries in the country, has to table its report in the House of Commons where all MPs have the right to stand up and speak on behalf of their constituents and bring up objections which they may have to the proposed boundaries. I have lived through one of these commissions. I do not know whether many of the newly-elected MPs have had the same experience.
I lived through one several years ago. I would like to tell Hon. Members a bit about how these commissions work.
A Bill is passed in the House of Commons and an electoral boundaries commission is set up. Commissioners are appointed in each province. Before they hold hearings they consider the results of the last census. They take the Act of Parliament which requires them to increase representation in the House to accord with the increase in population as contained in the last census. They consider the existing boundaries of existing constituencies and go about their work. They sit in some office building some place and spend several months drafting the boundaries of the constituency according to Parliament's wishes and according to the changes in the population as represented by the last census. The results of their work are then published. The day on which one receives a new map of one's constituency is quite a day for a Member of Parliament. Sometimes half of one's constituency has been taken away, and other times it is even more than half. There have been cases where whole constituencies have been wiped out as a result of movements and changes in populations, not only in provinces but in cities. As an example, in my City of Montreal, the east end of that city has lost 100,000 people over the course of the last 10 years. These people have moved to the West Island, to the South Shore and to Laval. There have been tremendous shifts of population within the Island of Montreal.
The commissioners perform their work based upon these shifts in population. They then table the new riding boundaries at which time the public finds out in some cases that a constituency is no longer there or that it has been moved a couple of miles away.
I conclude by saying that when the work of the commission is done it is only fair that parliamentarians have an opportunity to speak on behalf of their constituents and bring to the attention of the House their concerns with respect to the proposed changes. Under existing legislation an opportunity is provided for full debate on the changes proposed by electoral boundaries commissioners. Under the Bill which is before us the governing Party which upholds democracy and the parliamentary process removes the possibility of debate from the House of Commons. The Government now says that the report of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commissioners will be referred to a parliamentary committee and that this committee will have 30 days in which to study the report. After 30 days that is it, everything goes through. It does not matter if one has an objection. It does not matter if one is concerned about the work of the committee. It does not matter if as an MP you are concerned about the fact that your constituency has just disappeared. As an MP you have only 30 days to express your objections and then the law stands, as do the changes.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, if you regard this as a good example of the principle of democracy.

proposed an increase to 289. In fact, I agree with the Hon. Member of Lac-Saint-Jean that an increase of seven seats is acceptable. This would reflect what happened in the Committee and it is therefore more acceptable for those of us who sat on the Committee.
However, what worries me the most about the new proposal which would increase the number of seats from 282 to 295, which means an increase of thirteen rather than seven, is where these six additional seats will go. British Columbia will have two, and so will Alberta and Ontario. I do not want to be a bad sport and to seem envious of these provinces which are to receive additional seats. Let them have their seats! What worries me is that, while six seats are being added, not a single one will be for my province. This is not what had been suggested originally by the Committee. We could have fought about this in committee but that is not how it happened. It is therefore not surprising that the Quebec Members should rise, and I am happy to see that there are also Members on the Government side who share our concerns. I am going to try and speak as calmly as possible without making any partisan comments.
As it is often pointed out, Quebec is not like other provinces. That Province is the centre of French culture in Canada, and as such, whenever there have been redistributions, debates centering on the redistribution of seats, that point always has came up. And it must do so once again.
I say without being chauvinistic, it is clear that Quebec has a special role in Canada. It is the anchor point of the Frenchspeaking community. Furthermore it is the critical mass of the French-speaking community in Canada. I say it is the anchor point because minorities outside Quebec expect the latter to remain strong, because if Quebec does not survive as an entity, that is the end of the French-speaking community in Canada.
Of course this is disquieting. An increase of only seven seats, from 282 to 289 already was not too generous for Quebec. But if six other seats are to be added to that without a single one going to Quebec, someone has to speak up. I represent a Quebec constituency, and I could not face my constituents without at least having risen in this House. I am not sure this will change the views of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn). Ever since September 4th, last year, I have been getting used to constantly losing votes in this House. This is something that will happen again. As I said, I would not like Quebecers to say: When that was going on, our elected representatives were asleep. We are not asleep, our eyes are wide open, and we are trying to bring this home to the Government.
I am happy to see that we have the support of certain Quebec Members who, although from the Government side, as the Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean, have the courage to rise and point to what is going on. I am not yet sure what kind of result this will have, but it shows that Quebec Members from all sides of the House are alerted to what is going on and are looking for improvements.
You see, when we started discussing the issue in this House, Mr. Speaker, on second reading and then in committee, everyone agreed that we should alter a course which we from the Liberal Party had brought in through the amalgam method proposed here by Minister MacEachen and which, as we now realized that things have changed, would have brought upon quite a rapid increase in the number of Members in this House. But above all the Government is concerned with the matter of costs, and we must also realize that financially things are not what they used to be. Money is getting scarce.
However, if we start playing around with the amalgam formula and changing it, we automatically get another set of problems, because there was a very good reason why, according to the formula, the number of Members would increase very rapidly, as well as related expenditures. This was because the formula was intended to closely observe the basic principle of representation by population. And I must say that as soon as we get away from this method, which has its shortcomings, we automatically start tinkering with the principle of representation by population.
For instance, when the Government decides to include in the Bill before the House a measure ensuring that no province will lose a seat, even if according to census figures the population of that province has increased at a slower rate than in other provinces or even decreased.
Make no mistake: it is a kind of political protection the Government is giving itself, because if a province were in danger of losing a seat, and this happened about ten years ago in the House, I was there, and I am referring to the Province of Saskatchewan, well, there would have been an uproar. It was the Hon. John Diefenbaker, that famous Member from Saskatchewan, who objected.
However, one cannot expect to win on all counts when in Government. Where decisions are made, the political price has to be paid occasionally. Therefore, when the Government wants to obtain political protection, that is, assuring some provinces that they will not lose any seats even when their population is decreasing, this automatically comes up against the first basic principle as stated by the President of the Privy Council, that is, the principle of representation by population.
Once they refuse to accept that a Province may lose seats, for political reasons, and I understand that, they are in effect tampering with a basic principle. This is one of the things in that Bill I do not like.
Moreover, there already were other things in the Act about which there is very little we can do. We could always do something, but it would be difficult. There is the question of the Senate minimum. Prince Edward Island, for instance, should have one constituency based on its population. It has four, since it has four seats in the Senate. And the Constitution provides there can be no fewer Members of Parliament than Senators.
December 6, 1985

There again, this is a reality about which we are already departing from the basic principle of representation by population. So I submit that right from the start there were realities of that kind that were hard to cope with, without the Government stepping in to protect Provinces likely to lose seats. And when 1 say this, I am not thinking of any Province in particular. Quite possibly, the population in my own Province might some day, five or ten years down the road, increase at a slower rate than other provinces for all kinds of reasons. Quebec would then be the one to lose a seat. But, that's life. If we accept the principle of representation by population, we have to accept the consequences.
However, I do rise to protect my province when the formula is suddenly amended after the proceedings in Committee, to add six additional seats, none of which will come to my province and when, because we are a minority in this House, we certainly do not have the power to have this changed.
I therefore ask as sincerely as possible to the President of the Privy Council to reconsider his proposal to add six seats more than originally planned. If he would be so kind, so generous and so wise as to come back to his original proposal, under which the number of seats would increase from 282 to 289, he would avoid an extended debate in this House. He would have a better chance of gaining the support of the opposition parties. This is indeed why-
