PROVIDING DEFENCE OF THE ARCTIC ARCHIPELAGO Mr. Dave Nickerson (Western Arctic) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of providing adequate defence of the Arctic Archipelago.
National Defence
He said: Mr. Speaker, the intention this afternoon is to focus debate in this Chamber on the special question dealing with the defence of the far northern reaches of Canada. It is not a motion that is likely to be voted on by the very fact it is so broadly worded.
Not that long ago, Sir, 1 had the good fortune to tour parts of the Arctic with General David Battye in connection with the construction of the north warning system. 1 must say we were very well received wherever we went. People were pleased with the attitude of the new Government especially in those areas dealing with the maximization of local employment opportunities and local entrepreneurial opportunities with the new north warning system. We know that it is going to be done in a much different manner than with the old DEW line. During conversations with people at that time, we met with some who lived in areas north of the DEW line. To them, the DEW line was quite a way south. They said to us: "Are we not deserving of some form of defence in the area that we live? Is it right that in a case of attack the first element of any strategy is to abandon us to the enemy with the first line of defence being along the DEW line, located at roughly 70 degrees north?" I think they have a very good point. They deserve to be protected just the same as those living in metropolitan areas to the south.
It is not my intention this afternoon to be too critical of the Government because 1 know the Government has made vast improvements to our northern defences in just a short time over and above those of the previous Government which allowed defences to become rusty. There is no doubt about that at all.
Northerners were very pleased with the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) not that long ago in the context of Canadian sovereignty. The announcements made at that time will go to alleviate some of the deficiencies to which I have referred to quite an extent. For example, increased surveillance flights; more military exercises to be held in the North and of course, the construction of a Class 8 ice-breaker now underway. That ought to have been done a long time ago but was neglected by previous Governments.
I am not unmindful of the expenses that defence establishment cost. There is an obvious need for Canada to share those expenses with the United States of America. A good example of this is with the north warning system that comes as a result of the memorandum of understanding signed in Quebec City between the leaders of Canada and the United States last March.
We also must take into account special Canadian requirements over and above those of our friends to the south. My suspicion with respect to the north warning system is that if it were not necessarily a joint venture and that if cost were not such an important consideration, the north warning system would not follow the 1950s DEW line along the seventieth parallel, but rather it would go along the extremities of Canadian territory. The line would stretch from Inuvik in the west northeastward up to Alert at the top of Ellesmere Island,

December 6, 1985
National Defence
then possibly it would come down along the east coast of Ellesmere Island and Baffin Island, or it might even go around Greenland and come down the east coast of Greenland. There is valid criticism that can be made with respect to the north warning system, that we are superimposing 1980s technology on a 1950s geographical location. If we were able to do things in a way to maximize the Canadian interest, would it not be better, Mr. Speaker, to detect and engage enemy aircraft or enemy cruise missiles before they reach Canadian territory rather than to penetrate, in certain cases, many hundreds of miles into Canadian air space, over Canadian territory until being picked up by the DEW line? We could then launch successfully, I would hope, interceptor aircraft from locations even farther south than the DEW line and destroy the incoming threat. One of the difficulties is we would presumably be shooting down nuclear equipped missiles or bombers equipped with nuclear bombs over Canadian territory. Admittedly, it is not a densely populated area but the people who live there are of particular importance to me and my colleague because they are the people who vote for us. We feel if at all possible they should not be subjected to that type of threat.
The present detection system, the land-based radars that are necessarily used in the North are expensive, and we know that. Maybe we can improve our detection methods for the Arctic Archipelago by trying to improve the over the horizon back-scatter system that works in more southerly attitudes so that it can work in high latitudes. Presently it is affected by iones-pheric disturbances. If we could get over that problem, we would have a cheaper system for surveillance for detection in the very high Arctic. It is admitted the present north warning system is only an interim measure and that eventually the detection system will be satellite based, which will give us good coverage over the whole of Canada.
If we look at the existing military presence in the Arctic Archipelago we find there is very little there indeed. The only permanent military establishment is the communications research station at Alert. It can be noted, as an aside, that Alert is some 300 miles closer to Moscow than it is to Ottawa. There is not much else. There was another communications research base in Inuvik, not in the archipelago but close to it. That was closed or is in the process of closure right now.
Maybe we ought to think about the idea of having airports in the Arctic Archipelago from which F-18 aircraft could operate if the need arose. At the present time I can think of only one, the airport at Resolute Bay. There is one airstrip and no real alternate. Maybe some of the existing strips in the archipelago could be upgraded so that they could be used as forward operating locations.
There has been a continuing debate over whether or not you need a full-scale military base in the Arctic islands. I have never been able to determine whether or not that is necessary, but it is something about which military people have been talking for quite a number of years.
I should like to quote from an article which appeared in The Citizen of Ottawa in March, 1983. It was entitled "Canada needs military base in Arctic: ex-defence chief' and read:
Canada still needs the armed forces base in the far north that he promoted unsuccessfully in the early 1970s, General Jacques Dextraze, former chief of the defence staff, said Thursday.
Dextraze told the Senate subcommittee on national defence that "there is a great necessity to have a continuing presence up there."
The retired armed forces chief admitted that much of Canada's defence effort has to dovetail with planning by the United States for the defence of North America "but there are things that are purely national, things we must do as Canadians".
Dextraze said he selected Devon Island, on the Northwest Passage in the High Arctic, for the site of the proposed base-
The whole debate over what we need for the defence of the Arctic Archipelago has gone on for some time. It is not a new issue. I understand that Doctor Harriet Critchley has been an advocate of better defence of this area.
I have some quotations going back to October, 1981 from Le Droit to which I should like to refer.
[ Translation]
The Great North, a dent in Canada's armour.
-Brigadier-General Clay Beattie, DND Director General of Planning, said that if we were to neglect the north in might become the Maginot Line of the Atlantic Alliance.
And he goes on to say:
Colonel James Cameron, a retired officer who served in northern Canada, does not mince words. "I think it is absolutely shameful that we do not have more control over that region", said the former officer in a Toronto interview. Colonel Cameron is now on the board of the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies-

They are examples of where in years past this matter has been under debate by people who have given it a lot of thought.
The Arctic Islands are becoming increasingly important as a repository of strategic resources. There are vast oil and gas reserves which are in the process of being delineated in the Sverdrup Basin. There are billions of barrels of oil and trillions of cubic feet of natural gas. There were large hydrocarbon deposits in the Beaufort Sea, to the south of the area about which we are talking today. There were also mineral deposits in that area. In my opinion these assets are well worth protecting. There are also important shipping lanes in the area. The Northwest Passage is becoming a throughway, through the middle of the Arctic Archipelago.
It seems to me that military thinking in Canada has always been focused on Europe. We do not really give too much attention to the polar areas. Earlier this year, I had the opportunity to accompany the Secretary of State for External Affairs on a trip to the Soviet Union. Of course, they are very concerned with Europe over there, but at the same time they are giving a great deal of attention to polar matters. A lot of research is going on, some of which is presumably to increase the total of human knowledge, but not without military signifi-
December 6, 1985

cance at the same time. There is a lot of research into meteorology and there have been hydrographic surveys in the polar region. When we talk to senior Russian officials on the subject of possible conflict between the two superpowers, they immediately think in terms of action over polar areas. It is a state of mind which is very apparent over there, whereas in Canada it is something we tend to neglect and think in terms of traditional roles in Europe.
In case there was ever a conflict in polar areas, we have to try to think about what that might entail. Obviously, the first is the use of aircraft, missiles, in particular cruise missiles and bomber aircraft. We can neglect intercontinental missiles because they go away over the top. There are also some other things which might happen. There is the possibility of the occupation of the archipelago. At the present time it is not defended. It would be fairly easy to do that. What might happen is that if there was an altercation in Europe, a diversionary tactic such as the occupation of one or two communities in the archipelago could take place. The result of that would likely be that Canada would withdraw its troops from Europe in the face of public opinion and utilize them for the defence of the Canadian North. We have to take into consideration the possibility of using an attack on the Arctic as a diversionary measure. I would not like to see Arctic communities in that area being held hostage under those types of circumstances.
There is the idea of the archipelago surrounding seas being used as a submarine operating area. I refer to a May, 1983 article in The Citizen entitled "New attack subs planned to hunt Soviets in Arctic". The story is datelined Washington, and reads:
The U.S. Navy is designing a new attack submarine to hunt missile-carrying Soviet subs that operate extensively under the Arctic ice pack and use it as a sanctuary, the top navy commander said Wednesday.
Admiral James Watkins, chief of naval operations, said nuclear-powered 688-class Los Angeles attack submarines have put increased emphasis on patrolling under the ice to deny the Soviets a safe haven from which they could threaten America with nuclear attack.
Watkins described the ice pack as "a beautiful place to hide" for Soviet submarines equipped with intercontinental range nuclear-tipped missiles that could be used as a second or third-strike reserve force in the event of a nuclear war with the United States.
We have to think of the archipelago in all these terms. Unfortunately, the situation exists now with respect to naval warfare. At any rate, if there ever was a naval confrontation in the Canadian Arctic between the two superpowers, about all we could do as Canadians would be to sit on an ice floe and keep score.
I hope I have brought into context or focused attention this afternoon on the defence requirements of a very important part of Canada, a part of Canada which is becoming more important from day to day, a part of Canada of great strategic importance. In my opinion, today the Arctic Archipelago is an area which we should not and cannot neglect any longer from the point of view of defence of our nation.

Hear, hear!
National Defence

Mr. Speaker, I compliment the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) on bringing this motion before the House this afternoon. It gives us an opportunity to discuss the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. It is a very important subject in the eyes of Canadians as well as in the international community.
The Hon. Member would have been interested in being in Washington this week with the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. The Northwest Passage and other items were brought into focus in what really amounted to an all-Party, united debate in the State Department in Washington. It is too bad that that meeting was not able to go on the record.
Having commended the Hon. Member for bringing the subject before the House, there are two things that my Party would want to put on the record regarding our concerns that this motion not be used in an unlimited fashion to justify something else down the road. Just because we agreed with this blanket motion that was brought before the House by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, we do not want to find ourselves in a situation of agreeing to other things.
Number one, of course, is the reaffirmation that we do not want to see this motion used to allow participation in the Strategic Defence Initiative involvement in the North. I think perhaps the Hon. Member who brought forth this motion may very well be in agreement with that as well. In conjunction with that, we would not want this motion used to allow Government-to-Government research in SDI. I believe that issue was very well put to rest in the middle of 1985.
Our second major concern over the motion would be that we would not want this motion used in any way to involve Canada in any form of anti-ballistic defence. The Hon. Member touched upon that issue and mentioned in particular the problem that would exist in the case of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
In all honesty, I think the Hon. Member would agreed that the present Government has not done wondrous things for the northern part of Canada. He gives the Government full credit for having brought in the north warning system. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic knows very well, as does every well informed Canadian, that 90 per cent of the north warning system was already planned when the new Government took office. The new Government added such things as the forward-operating locations and it dressed it up a bit but basically, the entire north warning system was the product of the former Government. Let this Government not take credit for everything.
Conservative Members went around during the last election campaign saying that they would commit to a 6 per cent real increase in defence spending and they sent that propaganda into every mailbox of every member of the Armed Forces. Where do they stand on that issue today? The real growth in defence spending has been 2.92 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Where were the Liberals?

December 6, 1985
National Defence
When the Liberals were defeated on September 4, 1984, the real growth in national defence spending was 4.1 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: And the year before?

Let us go back to 1979 when the NATO Ministers agreed to 3 per cent real growth in spending on national defence. That was a NATO agreement. Canada and the United States are the only two countries out of the 15 countries that were members at the time that lived up to that 3 per cent real growth in defence spending. The only thing that is going to save this Government from putting a blemish on that record is inflation dropping enough to push real spending up over the 3 per cent level.
Members of the Government Party talked much about that commitment during the last election campaign. Since the election, both in the House and out, they have been using all kinds of rhetoric to build up the perception that they are doing wondrous things for the defence of the country. They should be ashamed of themselves for building up in the minds of the people the thought that they are doing great things.
1 was quite interested in a comment 1 heard from some members of the Armed Forces in Europe. About a month or two following the election, a new shipment of goods arrived in Europe. One corporal who was on hand said that it did not take the new Government long to start operating because all this new stuff was coming in already. Of course, that new stuff had been ordered by the previous Liberal Government a year or two ago. Everyone in the House knows how long it takes to receive equipment. With all the red tape involved in purchasing defence equipment, it is a good thing that we are not in a war.
Let us go a little further than that. New trucks of all sizes have been delivered to military bases across Canada and Europe. Those 2,761 two-and-a-half-ton trucks alone were ordered by the previous Government and the last of them have come on stream in the last year and a half. As well, there are the new tanks that were purchased by the Liberal Government. The Liberal Government purchased 18 long-range patrol aircraft, the best equipped and best working aircraft for our surveillance system over the North Atlantic that could possibly exist. Representatives of other NATO countries have looked at these new aircraft, gone up in them and they really like that package.
We want to remain aloof from star wars and ballistic missile defence systems so that we as a Canadian nation can retain our individuality in matters dealing with external affairs. As soon as we lose the sense of independence we have in forming our own foreign policy, then we will no longer have any influence on the other Parliaments of the world.
Let us return to the time when the tanker, the Manhattan, went through the North escorted by a Canadian ship. In the summer of 1985, the Polar Sea went through the North. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the American Secretary of State met in Washington three months before that voyage took place. What good did their discussions
do? The Amercians went ahead and sent the Polar Sea through Canada anyway. They would not listen to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As a result of the Manhattan voyage, the Americans knew that they could not dictate to then Prime Minister Trudeau on foreign affairs. If there is one thing that the Americans know for sure today, it is that Ronald Reagan has the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) in his hip pocket.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Horse feathers!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Rubbish!

I know that that bothers Hon. Members opposite but it is time that they recognized the facts of life.
The reason we should be seen as independent in our foreign policy is that Canada must continue to work toward an arms control agreement. The moment we are seen to be a dishonest broker in the middle of those nations in the world today, we will no longer have that influence to work with them in a constructive way. 1 think that Canada is the nation which should be out there leading the middle powers and, indeed, working closely with the Third World countries, to put the heat on the two major powers in the world to come to an agreement and to come to grips with their SDI programs. I want to be honest and realistic about this. Let us not always talk about the American SDI system when we talk about SDI. Let us also recognize the fact that even though one does not hear about it because it is bad propaganda, the Russians have their own SDI system on which they are doing research. We cannot go around as naive individuals in external affairs today. We need aggressive people on board. We need to have our own national independent policy on external affairs. We must have credibility in the eyes of the people with whom we are working. That credibility means that we be seen as our own person and as our own nation. 1 think that is extremely important today.
I wish to place on the record an excerpt from an article which appeared in Maclean's because I think it is important. This is an article which appeared in the November 2, 1985 issue of Maclean's with respect to a leaked document to Cabinet. The article states in part:
-Maclean's has learned that the federal cabinet has been presented with a package of sweeping proposals that would greatly expand Canada's military presence in the Far North-both as a demonstration of sovereignty aimed at impressing the United States and because of concern over Soviet submarine activity in the Canadian Arctic.
The proposals, outlined in a secret external affairs memorandum to cabinet, suggested a $4-billion program over the next decade to improve Canada's capacity to detect and attack foreign ships that infiltrate the nation's arctic waters. Among the proposals: between $2 billion and $3 billion for the construction of four nuclear-powered submarines that could operate for unlimited periods under the ice.
The memorandum also recommended a range of initiatives to upgrade Canada's surveillance of the Far North. These included the launching of a $350-million satellite designed to provide year-round radio images of the Northwest Passage, as well as the installation of underwater listening devices to monitor key bodies of water in the arctic archipelago and provide "trip wire" warnings of submarines passing through Canadian waters.
December 6, 1985

That is a good program as outlined. The only trouble with it is that someone leaked it from Cabinet and it has turned out to be somewhat of an embarrassment because the program was written up on the understanding that the money would come from existing funds. If $4 billion is to be taken from existing funds by this Government from whom will it be cut? Where else can this money be taken from? Will bases be closed up in Canada in order to pay for this program? Any program which is put forward without having the dollars to back it up is not really a serious proposal at all.
Having put my Party's conditions on the record and having said that we in the Liberal Party are interested in continuing to upgrade defences, we support the North Warning System, of course, wholeheartedly. We do so because, as 1 stated in my opening remarks, some 90 per cent of it is our product anyway. We are very much in favour of continuing purchases in conventional defence since we have made many of those in the last number of years.
1 think that in the field of external affairs we will have to make sure in the years ahead that we are our own person and that we do speak for Canada and that we do have our own individual external affairs policies. We must ensure that we press for arms control and that we work with other countries in the world. We cannot work as an individual but as a unit with other countries in the world in order to impress upon the two major powers that the only sane way to go, the only way for a sane society to go, is to sit down and come to arms agreements over the next few years. I hope that our Canadian Government will take this seriously. I hope that it will come forward with more dollars with respect to the purchase of conventional defence items in the country and that it will place emphasis on our reserve units in Canada, something with which I am in wholehearted support.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) for assisting me to catch a plane because I have to leave a few minutes early. I promise to refrain from any hostilities today toward my Liberal colleagues. In fact, I intend this speech to be non-hostile all around. I wish to thank and commend the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) for having brought this matter before the House for at least a short preliminary debate. His motion is very clear and to the point. I believe it has generated a very useful debate. The motion is simply:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing adequate defence of the Arctic Archipelago.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic has presented one version of the deterrent view and presented it quite well. Our Liberal colleague has presented another version of the same deterrent view. 1 wish to present the views of some people in Canada who are much concerned with that, because of where they live, who have still a different view.
I had the good fortune in September to go with the Standing Commitee on External Affairs and National Defence to Yellowknife to hear eight briefs of local residents there, beginning with the leader of the legislature and continuing through seven
National Defence
other briefs. I stayed in Yellowknife the second day rather than going up to Cambridge Bay and I forewent my per diem, as the rules require, because I wished to pursue also the question of housing in the Arctic. I was able to join with the Hon. Member for Western Arctic in a discussion of that a few weeks ago.
What I wish to present now is the gist of three of the briefs that the committee received that day: one from the Dene Nation and the Metis Association jointly; one from the Inuit; and one from the Committee for a Nuclear Free Western Arctic of the NDP.
1 think the most important of these is not, in fact, the brief from some Members of the New Democratic Party but, in fact, the brief of the Dene Nation and the Metis Association. 1 think Members may recognize that the recommendations they have put forward are not primarily involved in the dispute that we have here in what they call the "South". 1 understand that even Edmonton is way down south to the people in Yellowknife. So, of course, we are, I guess, close to the South Pole. But they do represent a people who have been here for many thousands of years, a people who have had a good deal of experience with war and with peace and with negotiation. Although they are a small group within Canada, the Dene, the Metis and the Inuit are, in fact, a majority of the population of the Northwest Territories, including the archipelago, about which the motion speaks.
I think the comments that they have made deserve to be heard by the Members of this House and by the Canadian public. Since the brief runs to several pages, I wish to give only the recommendations. Their first recommendation may seem rather trite at first. It is that the Canadian defence policy be reviewed in consultation with the Canadian public in an open forum. I say it may seem trite because the committee in which I am not able to participate most of the time is working very hard on doing just that consultation, or consultation covering a very important part of that. The reason the recommendation is not trite is because the open forum is not nearly so present as I believe the Dene and Metis people wish. That is one reason I wish to speak to it today.
The next three recommendations, I believe, give the heart of their point of view. The second recommendation states:
That those who wish Canada to pursue a policy of deterrence and co-operation through NORAD and NATO be invited to convince Canadians that that direction, or some variation of it, continues to be the correct one to take.
Hon. Members who have spoken have spoken on that assumption and with that view. The third recommendation states:
That those who support non-alignment and or neutrality be invited to convince Canadians that that direction or some variation of it, is the belter one to pursue.
The fourth recommendation states:
That the defence policy be reviewed and re-established before the next NORAD Agreement is signed.
1 believe that is a remarkadly useful statement in that it says clearly, in a few words, that we should debate the basic

December 6, 1985
National Defence
principles of our defence policy. I feel we should pay some attention to the Dene nation and the Metis Association. They gave consideration to the more specific aspects of the matter as well. They recommended that a soci-economic agreement on the north warning system be developed between Canada and the Government of the Northwest Territories. They agreed with the Government spokesman, with the Mayor of Inuvik, and with the Chamber of Commerce of Yellowknife, that people of the Northwest Territories should have a greater voice in what is done there. They go on to recommend:
The agreement should provide for a special advantage for northern workers and northern contractors to obtain jobs and business opportunities both during the construction stage and after completion. Training for the permanent jobs should begin immediately.
The sixth recommendation is:
That all aspects of the eight-year program of modernization of the DEW line be subjected to an environmental assessment and review process and provide information and assurances in the same way that is expected of industry.
Many others spoke to us that day about the same matter. They said that it is their land, they live there, and whatever defence policies are being carried out should take account of the people who live there. It is not a no-man's land.
They address the larger scene and recommend:
That Canada and all Canadians refuse to become involved in the U.S. Strategic Defense Initiative (Star Wars).
Not only the Canadian Government, as was the declaration made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but all Canadians should refuse to become involved.
The eighth recommendation is as follows:
That the Prime Minister undertake a "peace mission" to attempt to convince both the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. to stop their research and activity aimed at the militarization of outer space.
The ninth recommendation is as follows:
That if a new NORAD agreement is negotiated that a clause be included which states that Canadian participation does not include a commitment to take part in any Strategic Defense Initiatives and further does not include any commitment towards basing anti-ballistic missiles in the north or in Canada at any time in the future.
That is, again, a very plain declaration in which many Canadians are interested. 1 hope Canadians will understand that one of the representative bodies of Canada's first people has taken a very clear stand on that matter. They conclude by recommending:
That if a new NORAD agreement is negotiated that a termination clause of 12 months or less be included as it is in the 1981 agreement.
They state the "1981" agreement, but 1 believe it was 1980.
I believe the Dene nation and the Metis Association should be heard. I want to comment also on the brief of the Inuit. They did not speak so specifically as the Dene nation and the Metis Association but they did make some general points which ought to be heard. They say that for the Canadian Inuit, the fundamental concern is real participation in the development and implementation of Canadian policy in the Arctic with respect to national defence. They say that in terms of national defence, the Inuit form the front line of Arctic sovereignty and security. They do not want to find themselves
in no-man's land. They do want a stronger role in determining the fate of the Arctic.
The Inuit people through their organization have commented, and will continue to comment, and I hope we will listen to them. If an Inuit representative in Parliament wishes to speak on their behalf, I will listen to him with great interest, as I am sure will other Hon. Members of the House. In the few minutes I have left, I want to quote also from a brief which was prepared by the Nuclear Free Western Arctic Committee of the New Democratic Party. It is concerned with indications from Canadian, and particularly American publications, that the role of NORAD may be changed in the circumstances of SDI. It raised a question-

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's concern for relevance and I have chosen this material because it is relevant to the basic thrust of the motion with which we are dealing which concerns the type of military defence in the far north, specifically in the archipelago. That basic defence at present is proposed to be characterized primarily by NORAD, or by the north warning system, with what at present is an unclear and developing relationship to SDI. This concerns the archipelago as well as the whole of the Arctic. Therefore, the possibility that NORAD, the north warning system, and the archipelago will be involved not in protecting Canada against a first strike by the Soviet Union, but in responding to a second strike by the Soviet Union after a first strike by the United States, is very relevant to the people of the archipelago, as well as to the rest of the people of Canada. The point being made by this committee of residents in the Western Arctic is that the rule of NORAD in continental air defence must be re-examined in light of evidence which suggests that NORAD could play an integral part in provoking, not preventing, a nuclear war. This is of acute concern to people who are living in Mackenzie River Valley. I believe it is of equal concern to others who live in the Northwest Territories, including the archipelago. The committee went on to say:
In order to understand the role of NORAD in the 1980 and beyond it is necessary to consider American developments in nuclear weapons systems under the Reagan Administration. These include the MX land based missile, the Trident D-5 missile and the B-1B bomber. The NAVSTAR Global Positioning System, a satellite based navigation system soon to be in place, will ensure that these latest innovations arrive on target.
These technological developments, specifically the MX and Trident D-5 missiles, are particularly destabilizing in that their sophistication and accuracy give the Americans the confidence to strike at Soviet land based missiles and command posts with probable success.
What is under consideration there is a first strike. They go on to suggest that in that case the role of NORAD is not to
December 6, 1985

protect North America against a first strike whether it is based on the land perimeter of the Arctic or on the perimeter of the archipelago, but that the role of NORAD would then be only to defend Canada against a second strike by a Soviet missile or bomber force that would have been decimated, but not totally destroyed, by an American first strike. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, they recommend that the review of Canadian participation in NORAD should ascertain the degree to which present arrangements contribute to the support of an American counterforce first strike and to strategic defence. Canada should end its involvement in any activity that furthers these aims.
Those briefs were presented to our committee and were available for public review. I would urge Members of the House and members of the public to consider the opinion of those people who are representative of quite a number of the people who live in our Arctic areas, including the archipelago.

Mr. Speaker, with the short amount of time remaining I will only attempt to make a few comments, and not necessarily to use up the remaining time. I do wish to make a few brief comments in relation to the position of the Inuit because that has been mentioned quite a few times. After all, the subject matter of the motion of the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) is concentrated in my riding.
There are two basic representations which are normally made. First, from the special interest point of view, presentations to any governmental agency are normally prepared by consultants. What the consultants say, and what the people actually wish to say, are usually two different things altogether. Unfortunately, in Canadian political circles we normally hear what the consultants and politicians have to say. I participated in a seven-community tour from Inuvik to Pelly Bay this fall and I visited some of the high Arctic communities this summer when the issue of the Polar Sea first came up.
What I will be saying may never have been said before by a politician. When 1 was in Pond Inlet and Arctic Bay this summer an old Inuit told me that during World War II when they were issued with old .303 rifles and some rounds of ammunition they were instructed that if they saw any suspicious looking people, presumably Germans or other enemies, they were to shoot them. They took those instructions very seriously.
Professional Canadians or writers may not think much of that. In fact, I read a comment in News of the North by some people who made a bit of fun about the old-time "rangers" as they are called and how they were referred to as the first line of defence and what the heck could they do with cruise missiles anyway.
The point which I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that the Inuit in the central Arctic and high Arctic have said that they appreciate very much what the Canadian Government is doing for them because they know that they cannot defend them-
National Defence
selves with Russia being to the north of them. They appreciate Canadians spending millions of dollars to defend their area as well as Canadians in the south. Many of the older Inuit people are very nationalistic as far as the military is concerned. It is unfortunate that all we ever hear about are those on the negative side.
If I correctly understand comments of other politicians and Canadians in general, I believe they are saying that they want only to give the Armed Forces the ability to say: "The Russians are coming, the Russians are coming", and not the ability to do anything about it. We call ourselves a nation and yet we do not even want to be able to defend ourselves. We only want to be able to tell our neighbours to the south that the Russians are coming or that their cruise missiles have been fired.
Is that all that we want to do as Canadians? I wish that those who have more of a say on this issue would understand this side of the argument. Every time there is any form of Canadian military activity there are demonstrations in the streets and on the parliament grounds. We must decide whether we wish to be able to defend our own country.
As I mentioned before, I do want to give some of my colleagues an opportunity to speak so I will conclude my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I offer a few comments in this debate. I am sorry that the hour is so near to five o'clock. I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), for bringing this very important matter before us. I also appreciated the remarks of the Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk).
I am sorry that the Liberal critic did not stay around after his few remarks as I had a few comments that I wanted to direct his way. He was busy taking credit for the north warning line. I am sure you need not be reminded, Mr. Speaker, that the country had 23 years of comment and very little action. In the Liberal Party's concern for defence there is a lot of talk and no action. We took office and we took action. The Liberal Member also spoke with pride about the fact that no one could tell his former Leader, Mr. Trudeau, anything. I agree. Had he stayed long enough, in 1984 the people would have told him something that he could not have ignored. However, he left his Party to reap its rewards.

It was always a matter of great concern to me and to my naval colleagues that our capacity to function in the Arctic was negligible.
